description: We are LunaVision, a team at NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026 taking on the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. Our project, SELENE, helps lunar mission planners compare south-pole landing sites and dates by showing when a lander will have sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for communication, and how a launch delay changes that.
summary: SELENE is a working web tool that helps mission planners choose where and when to land near the Moon's south pole. There, the Sun and Earth sit low on the horizon, so nearby hills can hide them for days. Without the Sun a lander loses power; without Earth it loses its direct link home. A planner picks one of 12 ready-made sites, a landing time in UTC and a mission length. SELENE shows when the lander will see the Sun and reach Earth, gives a plain-English Good/Marginal/Poor verdict, and shows what changes if launch slips by hours or days. It also ranks the best landing dates and sites and compares plans side by side. It is built on NASA data: JPL Horizons positions of the Sun and Earth seen from the lunar surface, LRO LOLA terrain for each site's skyline, and NASA Deep Space Network dish geometry. This turns days of manual analysis into a quick, explainable check before a site or date is chosen.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SELENE answers one practical question for a lunar south-pole mission: "If we land here, at this time, will we have sunlight for power and a line to Earth for communication, and what changes if we are late?"

- Plan: choose one of 12 ready-made south-pole and comparison sites, a landing time (UTC) and a mission length (3, 7, 14 or 30 days). SELENE reports the share of time in sunlight, the longest stretch of darkness, the Sun's height above the local hills, the share of time with a two-way Earth link, the longest silence, ground slope, and a plain-English Good / Marginal / Poor verdict.

- What if launch is late: one click shifts the landing by +6 h, +24 h, +7 days or a custom delay and shows the planned and late plans side by side. Example from the live site: at Mons Mouton Plateau, a 14-day mission landing 17 Dec 2026 00:00 UTC is Good; a 7-day slip turns it Poor, with 158 hours (6.6 days) of darkness.

- See why: a 3D view of the real terrain around the site with Sun and Earth directions, a lander's-eye view, and an hour-by-hour timeline of Sun, Earth in view, Earth link and an illustrative battery level.

- Best dates: a verdict for every landing day from 1 Dec 2026 to 1 Feb 2028.

- Best sites: all sites ranked for the chosen date.

- Compare: plans side by side, with the best value marked in each row.

- How it works: an in-app page explaining the method, the data and the limits.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Ephemeris: a Python pipeline asks the NASA JPL Horizons API (DE441) for the azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth as seen from each site on the lunar surface.

2. Terrain: it builds each site's skyline from layered NASA LRO LOLA elevation models (5-20 m near the pole, coarser farther out), every 0.05 degrees of azimuth.

3. Visibility: the Sun or Earth counts as visible when its disc clears that skyline. This gives the Sun and Earth time windows.

4. Earth link: a two-way link exists when at least one NASA Deep Space Network 70 m dish (Goldstone DSS-14, Canberra DSS-43, Madrid DSS-63) is above the lander's skyline and the lander is above that dish's minimum elevation. Station data follows the NASA DSN Telecommunications Link Design Handbook (810-005).

5. Results are pre-computed into compact per-site files. The web app clips these windows to any landing time and mission length, intersects them, and turns them into verdicts, rankings and comparisons in the browser, with no server needed.

BENEFITS

At the lunar south pole, sunlight and Earth contact change hour by hour and depend on local hills. SELENE lets a planner compare sites and dates in seconds instead of days of manual analysis, see the cost of a launch delay before it happens, and understand every result in plain words backed by the underlying numbers.

INTENDED IMPACT

Help mission planners, students and outreach teams make safer, explainable landing choices for Artemis-era south-pole missions, where power and communication margins decide whether a lander survives. Next steps: custom coordinates, re-validation against NASA PGDA illumination maps, and a headline "hours with both sunlight and Earth in view in the first 72 hours" result for every delay.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python (NumPy) for the data pipeline; TypeScript, React 18 and Vite for the web app; Three.js for the 3D terrain view; Vitest for tests; GitHub Pages for hosting. Optional in-app assistant "Luna" uses the Google Gemini API through a small Node server. No hardware.

Live site: https://abowarda0.github.io/selene-lunar-navigator/

Source code: https://github.com/yossefhady/selene-lunar-navigator

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- It turns complex orbital and terrain geometry into a one-line verdict anyone can read, while keeping every number one click away.

- The "what if launch is late" comparison shows a delay's real cost, not just one snapshot.

- The lander's-eye 3D view lets users see why the Sun or Earth disappears behind real lunar hills.

- The AI assistant can only reword numbers SELENE has already computed: the site rejects any answer containing a number not shown on the page, so it cannot invent results.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy: real NASA ephemeris and terrain data, with the whole Sun and Earth discs checked against the skyline, not just their centres.

- Communication realism: a direct-to-Earth link needs a real DSN dish in view, not only Earth above the horizon.

- Honesty: Good / Marginal / Poor are our team's planning rule of thumb, not a NASA standard; the Earth link is geometry only, not a booked antenna; battery presets are illustrative; site samples are labelled as samples, not official landing sites; the current fine-terrain engine has not yet been re-checked against NASA PGDA maps (an earlier version was).

- Usability: no install, works in the browser, plain language, and every time shown in UTC.

- Scope: 12 pre-computed sites in this prototype; custom coordinates are planned.
